Two weeks ago I introduced our new client as "Mr Mehra" on a video call. His name was Mehta. I heard it the second it left my mouth, and I spent the whole weekend replaying it. By Sunday night I'd decided never to speak first in a meeting again.
On Monday, waiting for the lift, I tried an odd exercise. I asked myself what I remembered about my colleagues' mistakes. Ayesha had once shared the wrong screen in a call. When? I had no idea. Someone had mixed up two dates in a report. Who? Blank.
If I couldn't remember theirs, they probably weren't keeping a file on mine. Everyone was busy with their own slides and their own nerves.
So I made myself a small rule: speak, and if something comes out wrong, correct it and move on. I'm Hansa, I say "Mehra" sometimes, and the meetings keep going.

qa.q: What name did Hansa use for the new client?
qa.a: Hansa introduced the client as 'Mr Mehra' on a video call, when his name was Mehta.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling over the weekend after the call?
qa.a: Hansa felt mortified, replaying the slip all weekend and deciding never to speak first in a meeting again.

qa.q: What rule does Hansa make, and why does it help?
qa.a: Speak, and if something comes out wrong, correct it and move on; it gives permission to be imperfect instead of going silent.

qa.q: How might Ayesha remember that video call?
qa.a: Ayesha probably barely remembers it, just as Hansa couldn't recall when Ayesha shared the wrong screen.

In her first three stand-ups Minakshi said almost nothing. After one meeting she told me she had mixed up two ticket numbers and was sure the whole team now thought she was careless.

At the next stand-up she gave a full update, stumbled on a server name, said "sorry, the Pune server," and carried on. Nobody reacted.
Next step: I've asked her to lead Friday's demo. She agreed, and wrote "imperfect is fine" on her notebook cover.

Abhinav, you think your lucky socks win matches? Let me tell you about my lucky stone.
When I was your age, our village played football against the next village every Bohag Bihu. One year I found a smooth white stone by the river and kept it in my pocket. We won. Next Bihu I carried it again. We won again. By then I was sure the stone was our best striker.
The third year, on match morning, it was gone. I cried behind the granary. My legs shook so much I missed an easy pass.
At half-time our captain grabbed my shoulders. "Bhupen, you trained all month. Your legs know. The stone doesn't."
I played the second half thinking only about the ball. We drew, but I scored.
The stone turned up a week later, in my mother's washing basket.

qa.a: The captain's reminder that Bhupen's legs knew the training, not the stone, shifted the focus to the ball, and Bhupen scored.

Nikita, you asked why I never joke about betting. Sit.
When I was twenty-five, my closest friend at the mill, a quiet fellow, got into the races at Mahalaxmi. First Sunday, he lost a little. Second Sunday, he doubled it. "My luck will turn, Raghav," he'd say. "It has to." Soon he was borrowing from the canteen boy.
I did the clever thing first. I explained probability to him with a pencil on a newspaper. He nodded and went back the next Sunday.
So I stopped being clever. One evening I walked him home and said, "I'm frightened for you. I don't care about the odds. I care about you. Will you come with me to the mill's welfare officer, who helps people with this?"
He cried right there on the footpath. And he came.
He's seventy now, and he still sends me mangoes every summer.
